Lessons.Title: Distances and Parabolas
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Model a parabola as points equidistant from a focus and a directrix, and determine whether named points satisfy the locus.
Parabola is set of points equidistant from fixed focus and line directrix Use perpendicular distance to the line Focus (0,2), directrix y=−2 produces x²=8y

The distance from a point (x,y) to a horizontal line y=d is |y−d|: draw the shortest perpendicular segment to the line. In this case the point-to-directrix distance is |y+2|. The focus-to-point distance is √(x²+(y−2)²); the parabola consists of the points where these distances are equal.

Teacher rubric (0–8): four 0/1/2 teacher-scored criteria cover original focus/directrix equidistance including perpendicular line distance, source F2,2 and P6,5 proof with focus movement/open direction, original F6,4 point tests sqrt26 vs5 and10 vs10, and nine source Practice with exact selection B/E and exceptional focus-on-line case.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 6 Lesson 7, CC BY 4.0. Original Edulytiks problems; no copied source illustrations or restricted assessments.

Source 7.1 Notice and Wonder Distances (10 min): present a FIRST-PARTY graph with one marked focus and an actual labelled directrix; students write at least one independent notice and one wonder about the equal-length focus-to-curve and perpendicular-directrix-to-curve segments before teachers name the locus. A parabola comprises ALL points P satisfying distance(P,F)=PERPENDICULAR distance(P,line), not distance to an arbitrary point on the line; circle instead has fixed distance to centre alone. The original publisher illustration remains teacher-reviewed and is not duplicated.

Source 7.2 Into Focus (15 min): when directrix y=0 and focus F=(2,2), the vertex is midpoint of perpendicular focus-to-line segment V=(2,1), curve opens UP. Source P=(6,5) has directrix distance5 and focus distance sqrt((6−2)^2+(5−2)^2)=sqrt25=5, hence P lies on curve. Moving focus farther from fixed directrix widens the parabola (less curvature), bringing them closer narrows it; a focus BELOW the x-axis produces downward opening. In general if focus(a,p) and directrix y=d with p≠d, vertex(a,(p+d)/2) is closest point to focus AND directrix on symmetry axis x=a. Use first-party paper sketches when original digital applet is not connected. A second original source teacher synthesis F=(4,5), directrix y=1 yields vertex(4,3); source B directrix distance6.5 equals focus distance6.5 if actual B coordinates match publisher figure, teacher must check those coordinates.

Source 7.3 On Point (10 min): source focus F=(6,4), directrix y=0; candidate(11,5) has focus distance sqrt(5^2+1^2)=sqrt26, directrix distance5, so NOT on curve despite its appearance. Candidate(14,10) has focus distance sqrt((14−6)^2+(10−4)^2)=sqrt100=10 and perpendicular line distance10, so ON. A general point(x,y) is on this particular parabola iff sqrt((x−6)^2+(y−4)^2)=|y|, equivalently (x−6)^2+(y−4)^2=y^2; compare S exactly rather than approximating. Algebraic simplification (x−6)^2=8(y−2) is a valid independently-derived consequence but formal general equation belongs to following lesson.

Source 7.3 optional extension with focus F=(2,5) moved to F'=(2,2) and directrix y=0: vertex moves from(2,2.5) to(2,1), and parabola gets NARROWER when focus approaches the line (coefficient1/(2*focus-height) gets larger). If focus lies directly ON directrix, equal-distance locus degenerates to a straight line perpendicular to directrix THROUGH focus, not a nondegenerate parabola (the x=2 line in this setup). State separate boundary case rather than claiming vertex at midpoint still defines genuine parabola.

Source lesson synthesis focus(-1,3), directrix y=1 gives vertex(-1,2); source P=(3,6) directrix distance|6−1|=5 but its focus distance sqrt((3+1)^2+(6−3)^2)=sqrt25=5, so P is ON. Horizontal directrix y=d has point distance |y−d| with absolute value, and point-to-focus needs Pythagoras. Source student summary distinct focus(2,1), directrix y=−3 has vertex(2,−1), and example F=(2,3), directrix y=1, P=(−2,6) has distances5 and5 and lies on curve. Preserve earlier correct independent RichV2 examples focus(0,2) directrix y−2 gives x²=8y, and F=(3,5), line y1 gives vertex(3,3), but do not substitute for original source tasks.

Source Practice P1-P9: P1 P=(6,y), focus(4,1), x-axis directrix: equation (6−4)^2+(y−1)^2=y^2 gives y=5/2=2.5. P2 focus(6,2) and directrix y=4: B(2,−1) focus5 and line5, E(8,2) focus2 and line2 are ON, A(1,−2),C(6,2),D(7,3) are NOT; options B,E only. P3 focus(0,4) vs y0 vertex(0,2) opening up/wider, focus(0,−6) vs y0 vertex(0,−3) opening down and wider due larger focus-line separation. P4 circle x²+y²−8y+5=0 becomes x²+(y−4)^2=11, centre(0,4), radius sqrt11. P5 boxes x²+14x→49 choice2, x²−0.5x→1/16 choice1, c²−10c→25 choice3, z²+z→1/4 choice4; A2 B1 C3 D4. P6 squares (x−6)^2,(y+4)^2,(w−8)^2. P7 circle centre(1,−4) radius10 gives (x−1)^2+(y+4)^2=100. P8 soap prism5.6cm×13cm×16cm volume1164.8cm³, mass1.048kg=1048g, density1048/1164.8≈0.8997g/cm³ <water1, so floats in simplified source rule. P9 two circles of equal radius centred at B, with A and D on same circle along rays BA and BC, ensure BA=BD; perpendicular bisector of AD contains B, and in isosceles ABD it bisects vertex angle B. The construction works if D is the source ray-circle intersection, A≠D and original intended angle orientation, and if all points truly lie in plane. Original 7.4 Point and a Line locked cooldown not claimed copied; independent first-party paper human scored.

KeyConcepts.Title: Focus-directrix
KeyConcepts.Definition: Parabola is set of points equidistant from fixed focus and line directrix
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use perpendicular distance to the line

KeyConcepts.Title: Distance-to-line
KeyConcepts.Definition: The perpendicular distance from point (x,y) to a horizontal line y=d is the absolute value of their vertical-coordinate difference.
KeyConcepts.Rule: distance((x,y),line y=d)=|y−d|; this number is nonnegative.
KeyConcepts.Example: For P=(4,2) and directrix y=−2, the distance is |2−(−2)|=4.

KeyConcepts.Title: Vertex
KeyConcepts.Definition: The point halfway between focus and directrix on symmetry axis

WorkedExamples.Title: Distances and Parabolas: problem 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Find equation focus (0,2), directrix y=−2.
Steps: For P=(x,y), the distance to focus (0,2) is √(x²+(y−2)²), and distance to directrix y=−2 is |y+2|.
Equate and square these nonnegative distances: x²+(y−2)²=(y+2)².
WorkedExamples.Check: For x=4 the equation gives y=2; the focus and directrix distances are both exactly 4.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distances and Parabolas: problem 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Is P=(4,2) on this parabola?
Steps: Compute the perpendicular directrix distance: |2−(−2)|=4, hence squared distance 16.
Because both distances equal 4, P=(4,2) is on the focus-directrix parabola.
WorkedExamples.Check: The point satisfies x²=8y, since 16=8·2; both directrix and focus distances equal 4.

Lessons.Title: Equations and Graphs
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Derive and graph a parabola equation from focus/directrix information, matching its vertex, orientation and parameter p.
(x−h)²=4p(y−k) for p≠0 Focus (h,k+p) and directrix y=k−p p>0 opens up
(y−k)²=4p(x−h) Focus (h+p,k), directrix x=h−p Confirm by equidistance, not picture alone

Teacher rubric (0–8): four 0/1/2 human criteria score source three focus distances without prematurely using Pythagoras, complete source focus3,2 directrix y0 derivation and graph, four source-aligned teacher-verified card pairings and distinction from ellipse optional, and 8 source Practice exact answer choices with unavailable P8 figure caveat.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 6 Lesson 8, CC BY 4.0. Original Edulytiks problems; no copied source illustrations or restricted assessments.

Source 8.1 Focus on Distance (5 min): original parabola focus F=(-2,2), directrix y=0 (x-axis), and original labelled P_A=(2,5), P_B=(-8,10), generic P_C=(x,y) on curve. Students find focus distances by definition WITHOUT first using Pythagoras: d(A,F)=5, d(B,F)=10 and d(C,F)=|y|, which on an upward parabola is y. Later independently confirm d(A,F)=sqrt(4²+3²)=5, d(B,F)=sqrt((-6)²+8²)=10. Label perpendicular to LINE, not diagonal distance.

Source 8.2 Building an Equation for a Parabola (20 min): original focus(3,2), directrix y=0, for arbitrary point P=(x,y) equate NONNEGATIVE distances sqrt((x−3)²+(y−2)²)=|y|. Square both sides: (x−3)²+(y−2)²=y². Expand and solve: (x−3)²+y²−4y+4=y² => (x−3)²=4(y−1), or y=(1/4)(x−3)²+1. Vertex(3,1), positive p=1 and parabola opens UP. Check source point at vertex both distances1, plus P=(5,2) on parabola because (5−3)²=4*(2−1). All steps must preserve equality; source expects derived SPECIFIC equation, not memorization of a general p-parameter formula.

Source 8.3 Card Sort Parabolas (10 min): source publisher card blackline graphics are teacher-protected and no A–H original graph/equation labels are available in accessible task text; use first-party four contrasting cards, with focus, directrix, vertex, orientation and coefficient matching, teacher scores paired justification, but do not pretend to match unavailable original publisher labels. First-party cards examples original 8.2 y=.25(x−3)²+1; source lesson summary focus(1,4), directrix y0 gives y=(1/8)(x−1)²+2; focus(-1,-7), directrix y3 gives y=−(1/20)(x+1)²−2; and original source 7.3 focus(6,4), directrix y0 gives y=(1/8)(x−6)²+2. Explain a narrower curve has greater |a| when vertex matched.

Source 8.3 OPTIONAL extension: points only HALF as distant from focus(5,3) as from directrix y=0 mean sqrt((x−5)²+(y−3)²)=|y|/2 (distances nonnegative). Squaring yields 4(x−5)²+4(y−3)²=y², or 4(x−5)²+3(y−4)²=12. The locus is an ELLIPSE (x−5)²/3+(y−4)²/4=1, not a parabola, and no real point with arbitrary positive x,y outside this ellipse qualifies. Original source asks students to sketch with graphing technology; if not connected require hand sketch or teacher-verified first-party graph, not a claim of live Desmos.

Source lesson synthesis circle centre(6,3) radius2 equation (x−6)²+(y−3)²=4; source parabola same focus(6,3) and directrix y=1 equation (x−6)²+(y−3)²=(y−1)², which simplifies y=(1/4)(x−6)²+2. Both describe equal distance to a point on left, but circle fixes radius, parabola fixes distance to a line. Student summary different focus(1,4) and line y0 yields (x−1)²+(y−4)²=y² and y=(1/8)(x−1)²+2. Preserve earlier correct independently authored RichV2 examples focus0,3/directrix y−3 x²=12y and horizontal parabola examples; they are distinct from source's original focus3,2.

Source Practice P1-P8: P1 x²+y²−8x+4y=29 represents CIRCLE choice A because (x−4)²+(y+2)²=49, centre4,−2 radius7. P2 focus(4,1), directrix y0: (x−4)²+(y−1)²=y², equivalently y=.5(x−4)²+.5. P3 focus(−1,−7), directrix y3: true focus-distance equation B (x+1)²+(y+7)²=(y−3)² and vertex form E y=−(1/20)(x+1)²−2, NOT coefficient−20 or sign+2. P4 source parabolas focus A(3,2) vs B(5,4) with same y0 directrix: B wider (height4 bigger) and symmetry line x5 to RIGHT of x3; choices B and E. P5 focus(5,1), directrix y=−3 vertex(5,−1). P6 x²+7x needs49/4=12.25 choice C. P7 factor x²+3x=x(x+3); x²−6x−7=(x−7)(x+1); x²+4x+4=(x+2)². P8 original 2D region rotated about shown vertical axis has marked dimensions only source illustration; teacher must inspect source picture before assigning volume. WorkedExamples.Title: Two lines perpendicular to a third
WorkedExamples.Question: Lines ℓ: y=2x+1 and n: y=2x−3 are each perpendicular to m: y=−x/2+4. Prove ℓ∥n.
Steps: The slope of m is −1/2 and the slope of each of ℓ and n is 2.
Both products are 2·(−1/2)=−1, so each line is perpendicular to m.
The intercepts of ℓ and n differ (1 and −3), so they are distinct lines with equal slope and therefore parallel.
WorkedExamples.Answer: ℓ and n are distinct parallel lines.
WorkedExamples.Check: The proof uses both perpendicularity and distinctness, not an unlabelled sketch.
